name: Roger's Vitalator

lead: Roger's Vitalator was a mains-powered electromedical instrument made in London in 1925 by Ideal Home Electrical Appliances Ltd. It sent a high-frequency, low-voltage current through glass vacuum electrodes placed on the body.

It came with many attachments, including a comb for scalp and hair loss and a surface electrode for skin and facial treatment, and was promoted as a beauty aid as well as a remedy for warts, aches and deafness. Today it is a museum object.

paras: The user plugged it into the mains, set voltage and power dials, and moved a glass electrode over the chosen area. The sensation ranged from gentle warmth to a sharper sparking feeling. The maker said the current enriched blood and lymph flow.

The museum record notes that such devices fell out of fashion by the 1950s as the health claims were recognised as unfounded. Mains-powered high-frequency devices of this era carried electrical and burn hazards in general.

lead: Roger's Vitalator was an electromedical instrument made in 1925 in London by Ideal Home Electrical Appliances Limited, held today by the Science Museum Group.[1] It housed a high-frequency, low-voltage generator in a wooden case with two dials controlling voltage and power.[1]

The treatment was delivered through glass vacuum electrodes, with about 50 attachments available. A kit in the museum collection includes a comb for scalp and hair loss, a surface electrode for skin and facial treatment, a metal electrode for weak nerves and an electrode for haemorrhoids.[1] It was marketed for warts, hair loss, aches and pains and deafness, and as a beauty aid.[1]

The maker claimed that the current increased the richness of the blood and lymph flow by constricting and then releasing blood vessels.[1] The museum notes that home electrical therapy devices were popular from the late 1800s to the mid-1900s and had fallen out of fashion by the 1950s.[1]

paras: The device plugged into the mains and delivered a high-frequency, low-voltage charge to glass vacuum electrodes. Sensations ranged from gentle warmth to sparking.[1] Case dimensions are 190 by 270 by 285 mm.[1]
Claims covered warts, hair loss, muscle and nerve pain and deafness, plus use as a beauty aid.[1] Promotional booklets from the company survive in museum collections.[1]

Electrical therapy devices rose when electricity was new and poorly understood by the public, and declined by the 1950s with medical advances and recognition that their health claims were unfounded.[1]
